    #CA1 S1 (2023 - 2024)

    #Question 1

    An airfoil is described by the following equation:

    cz​=ab(cx​)[1−a(cx​)2]

    where 0≤cx​≤1

    #Part (a)

    Determine the coefficient A0​ in terms of a and b.

    Using variable transformation cx​=21​(1−cosθ),

    0≤21​(1−cosθ)≤1

    0≤1−cosθ≤2

    0≥cosθ−1≥−2

    1≥cosθ≥−1

    0≤θ≤π

    Expanding the given equation,

    z=abx[1−a(cx​)2]

    z=abx−a2bc2x3​

    Differentiating with respect to x,

    dxdz​=ab−3a2bc2x2​

    dxdz​=ab−3a2b(21​−21​cosθ)2

    dxdz​=ab−3a2b(41​−21​cosθ+41​cos2θ)

    dxdz​=ab−43​a2b+23​a2bcosθ−43​a2bcos2θ

    A0​

    =α−π1​∫dxdz​ dcosθ

    =α−π1​∫0π​ab−43​a2b+23​a2bcosθ−43​a2bcos2θ dθ

    =α−π1​∫0π​ab−43​a2b+23​a2bcosθ−43​a2b(21​+21​cos2θ) dθ

    =α−π1​∫0π​ab−43​a2b+23​a2bcosθ−83​a2b−83​a2bcos2θ dθ

    =α−π1​∫0π​ab−89​a2b+23​a2bcosθ−83​a2bcos2θ dθ

    =α−π1​[abθ−89​a2bθ+32​a2bsinθ−163​a2bsin2θ]0π​

    =α−π1​(abπ−89​a2bπ)

    =α−ab+89​a2b

    Using the integral ∫cos2θ dθ=21​sinθcosθ+21​θ,

    =α−π1​[abθ−43​a2bθ+32​a2bsinθ−43​a2b(21​sinθcosθ+21​θ)]0π​

    =α−π1​[abθ−43​a2bθ+32​a2bsinθ−83​a2bsinθcosθ−83​a2bθ]0π​

    =α−π1​(abπ−43​a2bπ−83​a2bπ)

    =α−ab+43​a2b+83​a2b

    =α−ab+89​a2b

    #Question 2

    Source A, with a strength of 6 m2/s, is located at (0m, 2m).
    Source     B, with a strength of 4 m2/s, is located at (0m, 5m).

    #Part (a)

    Determine the location of the stagnation point.

    Source A: vrA​​=2πrA​QA​​

    where rA​ is distance from the center of A

    Souce B: vrB​​=2πrB​QB​​

    where rB​ is distance from the center of B

    At stagnation point, vrA​​=vrB​​.

    2πrA​QA​​=2πrB​QB​​

    rB​rA​​=QB​QA​​

    rB​rA​​=46​

    rA​=1.5rB​

    Distance between the sources is,

    y=5−2=3 m

    From the diagram,

    3=rA​+rB​

    3=1.5rB​+rB​

    rB​=1.2 m from the center of B

    With respect to the origin,

    Stagnation Point=(0m, 3.8m)

    #Part (b)

    Determine the velocity at the point (1m, 1m). State the direction.

    Resolving vrA​​ into u and v,

    uA​=vrA​​cosθA​=2πrA​QA​cosθA​​

    vA​=vrA​​sinθA​=2πrA​QA​sinθA​​

    Resolving vrB​​ into u and v,

    uB​=vrB​​cosθB​=2πrB​QB​cosθB​​

    vB​=vrB​​sinθB​=2πrB​QB​sinθB​​

    General equation for u.

    u=uA​+uB​

    u=2πrA​6cosθA​​+2πrB​4cosθB​​

    General equation for v.

    v=vA​+vB​

    v=2πrA​6sinθA​​+2πrB​4sinθB​​

    The unknowns are rA​, rB​, θA​ and θB​.

    From the diagram,

    rA​=12+12​=2​ m

    rB​=12+42​=17​ m

    θA​=tan−1(−1)=−45°

    θB​=tan−1(−4)=−76°

    Substituting the values into u and v,

    u=2π2​6cos(−45)​+2π17​4cos(−76)​

    u=0.51482 m/s

    v=2π2​6sin(−45)​+2π17​4sin(−76)​

    v=−0.62728 m/s

    Using Pythagoras theorem,

    VP​=0.514822+(−0.62728)2​

    VP​=0.81149 m/s

    Direction of velocity vector is,

    θP​=tan−1uv​

    θP​=tan−10.51482−0.62728​

    θP​=−50.624°

    Negative sign indicates clockwise from horizontal axis.
    Velocity vector is pointing     57.608° below the x-axis.

    #Question 3

    Delta wings are commonly found on high-speed aircraft. Explain why?

    • Delta wings generate counter-rotating vortex pair along the leading edge
    • Vortex is a source of high-energy flow → local static pressure above wing reduces
    • Low static pressure creates a “suction effect” on the top surface of the wing
    • Effect energizes flow over the wing and enhances lift

    #Question 2

    You are tasked to measure the turbulence intensity level of the wake at the trailing edge
    of a NACA0020 airfoil inclined at     α=25°. Which experimental technique do you use? Briefly describe the procedures and post-processing.

    A suitable technique is laser doppler anemometry. As we are only interested in the
    flow at the trailing edge of the airfoil rather than the flow around the entire airfoil,
    it is not required to measure the velocity field around the entire airfoil. Thus, point measurement is sufficient.

    Procedures of experimental technique:

    • Uses two laser beams of different frequencies to produce an intersection volume
    • An interference pattern is then created in that intersection volume
    • Tracer particles are released into the flow and entrained in the flow
    • Particles scatter light from the laser as they pass through the volume
    • Scattering of light causes a frequency shift (Doppler effect)
    • Frequency shift is proportional to the velocity of the particles

    Turbulence intensity level of the wake can be determined using,

    T.I.=U∞​urms​​

    where U∞​ is the freestream velocity of the flow and
    urms​ is the root mean square of the measured velocity

    #Question 3

    An aircraft with a finite tapered wing operating at 3° geometric angle of attack is to be designed based on a thin, asymmetric airfoil. If the zero-lift angle of attack of the airfoil
    is     −1.5°, and the induced drag factor δ=0.05, determine the minimum aspect ratio
    of the wing such that the wing’s lift curve slope is 70% of the airfoil’s lift curve slope.

    Recall from thin airfoil theory that the theoretical lift curve slope of
    an airfoil, symmetric or asymmetric (cambered), is a0​=2π/rad.

    Span effectiveness of the wing is,

    e=1+δ1​=1+0.051​=0.95238

    Lift curve slope of the wing is,

    dαdCL​​=0.7(2π)=4.3982

    Equating to the lift curve slope equation,

    dαdCL​​=1+πeARa0​​a0​​

    4.3982=1+π(0.95238)AR2π​2π​

    AR=4.9

    #Part (b)

    • Delta wings produce a pair of counter-rotating vortices over the wing
    • Vortices create a suction effect that energizes the flow over the wing
    • Lift generation is enhanced due to delayed flow separation
    • Vortices begin to breakdown at high α, which results in unsteady flow

    #Part (c)

    Single engine vs multiple engines:

    • Number of engines is dependent on the type of mission an aircraft is used for
    • Fighter aircraft can have either single engine or dual engines configuration
    • Single engine requires less internal volume (aircraft can be made compact)
    • Dual engines allow higher flight speeds/acceleration to be achievable
    • Commercial aircraft typically have multiple engines such that in the event of
      a single engine failure, aircraft is still capable of maintaining flight (ETOPS)
    • General aviation typically have a single engine due to costs

    Aerodynamics in the event of a single engine failure:

    • Loss of thrust on one side results in a yawing moment
    • Rudder needs to be deflected in the direction opposite of yaw
    • Deflection of rudder will also increase drag of the aircraft
    • Lift remains unchanged as long as flight speed is maintained

    #Part (d)

    • Flaps increase lift while also increasing drag of the aircraft
    • Increased drag during takeoff increases the runway length required
    • More fuel is burned to overcome drag so as to attain required liftoff speed
    • Increased drag during landing is desirable as it reduces the landing distance

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Cause of fluttering:

    • Turbulent wake from the main wing
    • Vortices due to flow separation affect the stabilizers located downstream
    • Vortex frequency coincides with the natural frequency of the stabilizers

    Laser doppler velocimetry:

    • Two laser beams of different frequencies are used to create intersection volume
    • Interference pattern is produced in the volume (area of interest)
    • Tracer particles are introduced into the flow
    • As particles pass through the lasers, they scatter the light
    • Scattering of light causes a frequency shift (Doppler effect)
    • Frequency shift is proportional to the velocity of the particles
    • Fast Fourier transform is performed on the collected velocity data
    • Interval between spikes in the frequency graph gives the flutter frequency

    Advantages of method:

    • Non-intrusive
    • No calibration required
    • High frequency response
    • More accurate than hot-wire

    Disadvantages of method:

    • More expensive than hot-wire
    • Requires more setup preparation
    • Requires the use of tracer particles
    • Requires optical access for the lasers

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant, tracer particles
    • Laser light source is used to create a thin light sheet to illuminate area of interest
    • High-speed camera records the motion of suspended particles within this area
    • Cross-correlation is used to determine each particle’s velocity
    • Calculated velocity vectors are used to create velocity field of the flow

    Advantages of method:

    • Fast experiment
    • Non-intrusive
    • Global velocity measurement
    • Other variables can be derived

    Disadvantages of method:

    • Low frequency response
    • High storage requirement
    • Significant post-processing time
    • Each velocity vector is an average over the cross-correlation window

    #Part (b)

    • Shockwaves are pinned to the sharp edges, preventing them from oscillating
      up and down along the chord of the wing, which will result in unsteady flow
    • Sharp leading edges will eventually be eroded due to friction with moving air
    • Supersonic airfoil has small internal volume, and thus has less fuel storage
    • Small internal volume also reduces the space available for flight controls
    • Thin cross-section makes it difficult to design structural supports within it

    #Part (c)

    • Prevent ingestion of the fuselage boundary layer (slow, moving air)
    • Prevent ingestion of a turbulent fuselage boundary layer
    • Ingestion of these can cause a compressor stall whereby air becomes
      “stuck” in the compressor, which can result in an engine flameout
    • Engines prefer a laminar flow flow of air that is undisturbed

    #Part (b)

    • Flow separation may occur due to drastic change in contour of the inlet
    • As a result, flow becomes turbulent (presence of vortices)
    • Disturbed air may cause an engine stall

    #Part (c)

    • Modify the 30° diagonal contour into a smooth, curved contour
    • Curved inlet ensures laminar flow of air into the engine intake (no separation)

    #Part (d)

    • Engine is designed to only ingest subsonic air
    • Supersonic air will cause an engine flameout due to high volume flow rate
    • Flame holders in the combustion chamber will get blown out like a candle
    • Shocks at the inlet reduce speed of the intake air to prevent a flameout
    • Shocks produced are located forward of the inlet such that the shock
      does not propagate downstream into the inlet

    #Part (c)

    Drawback of a delta wing:

    • Delta wings tend to have their center of pressure located further aft
    • Location of cp results in a nose-down pitching moment
    • Lifting canard counteracts this inherent pitch moment

    Use of conventional tailplane:

    • Commercial aircraft tend to have cp located forward of center of gravity
    • In the event of engine failure, the aircraft will tend to nose-down
    • Tendency of nose-down prevents the occurrence of stall
    • In normal operation, tailplane counteracts this nose-down moment,
      such that the aircraft is able to maintain a steady level flight (cruise)

    #Part (d)

    • Flaps will increase profile drag due to an increase in frontal area
    • Flaps will also increase induced drag due to higher lift generated
    • Total drag of aircraft will ultimately increase
    • CD​=CD0​​+kCL​2

    #Part (b)

    #Part (i)

    Laser doppler velocimetry:

    • Two laser beams of different frequencies are used to create an intersection volume by overlapping the beams, which creates an interference pattern
    • Tracer particles are introduced into the flow (microspheres, oil droplets)
    • Tracer particles scatter the light as they flow through the area of interest
    • Scattering of light causes a frequency shift (Doppler effect)
    • Frequency shift is proportional to the velocity of the particles

    #Part (ii)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant, tracer particles
    • A laser light source is used to create a thin light sheet
    • Light sheet illuminates the particles flowing in the area of interest
    • A high-speed camera records the motion of the suspended particles
    • Cross correlation method is used to determine each particle’s velocity
    • Calculated velocity vectors are used to create a velocity field of the flow

    #Part (iii)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fast experiment (less setup preparation)
    • Non-intrusive technique (does not disturb the vortex cores)
    • Other variables can be derived from velocity measurements (vorticity)

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    • At zero α, the height of airfoil’s frontal area is approximately its thickness
    • Airfoil’s frontal area is at its smallest when α is zero, which corresponds
      to a positive value of CL​ since the airfoil is cambered
    • As α decreases, the airfoil’s frontal area increases
    • Increase in frontal area results in higher profile drag

    #Part (b)

    Undesirable effects:

    • Formation of shockwaves on the wing causes unsteady flow
    • Unsteady flow over the wing results in fluctuations in lift and drag
    • Unpredictable lift and drag reduces controllability of the aircraft
    • Back and forth movement of shockwaves can cause structural vibrations

    Transition from subsonic to supersonic flow:

    • A shockwave forms as the aircraft approaches sonic speed
    • Flow separation occurs downstream of the shockwave
    • Wake, and thus profile drag, of the wing increases
    • Section of the wing that can generate lift is reduced, thus lift decreases

    #Part (c)

    Wash-in configuration:

    • A wing with wash-in experiences spanwise flow towards the wing root
    • Slow, moving air accumulates at the wing root, creating a thick boundary layer
    • A thick boundary layer is more likely to separate from the surface of the wing
    • Flow separation at the wing root will increase the overall drag of the aircraft

    At high α, the wingtips will stall earlier than the wing root, which renders the
    outboard ailerons ineffective, and the pilot would have to rely on the inboard
    controls that are less effective due to a smaller moment arm.

    Wash-out configuration:

    • A wing with wash-out experiences spanwise flow towards the wingtips
    • A thick boundary layer is less likely to form, and flow separation is minimized
    • Fluctuations in lift and drag of the aircraft due to flow separation is prevented

    At high α, the wing root will stall earlier than the wingtips, ensuring the outboard ailerons maintain effectiveness, which is more ideal due to a longer moment arm.
    Thus, a smaller deflection is required to achieve the same effect.

    #Part (d)

    • Prevent ingestion of the fuselage boundary layer (slow, moving air)
    • Prevent ingestion of a turbulent fuselage boundary layer
    • Ingestion of these can cause a compressor stall whereby air becomes
      “stuck” in the compressor, which can result in an engine flameout
    • Engines prefer a laminar flow flow of air that is undisturbed

    #Part (e)

    • Unsteady shocks move up and down along the chord of the wing
    • Amount of flow separation downstream of the shock varies
    • Lift and drag fluctuates due to flow separation occurring at
      different points along the chord over a period of time
    • Reduced controllability of aircraft due to changing lift and
      drag, which requires different control inputs to the aircraft

    #Part (f)

    • Viscous fluid (theory assumes inviscid flow)
    • Thick airfoil (theory is based on thin airfoils)
    • High angles of attack (theory assumes small α)

    #Part (b)

    Explain why some aircraft are able to continue to fly “straight-
    and-true” at subsonic speeds even when they are upside down.

    • Cambered airfoil creates pressure difference between upper and lower surfaces
    • In inverted flight, as long as the airfoil has a positive angle of attack,
      lift generated by the wing acts in the opposite direction of weight
    • Cambered airfoil generates lift even at zero angle of attack
    • To maintain inverted flight, nose of aircraft must be pitched upwards, above the horizon, such that the lower surface becomes relatively parallel to incoming air

    Note that to maintain inverted flight for prolonged periods, the aircraft must have a positive feed fuel system such that engines continue to receive fuel in inverted flight.

    #Part (c)

    Some aircraft have twin rudders instead of a single rudder. What aerodynamic
    benefits do twin rudder configurations offer over single rudder configuration?

    • Twin rudders can be made smaller than a single rudder as they split
      the aerodynamic load, thus reducing the profile drag of the aircraft
    • Twin rudders provide extra control, especially at high speeds, where each
      rudder can deflect by a small amount to achieve a greater combined effect
    • Aircraft with wide fuselages (F15), benefit from control in high α, where the
      fuselage would otherwise block sufficient airflow to a single center rudder
    • Twin rudders can act as speed brakes by deflecting in opposite directions

    #Part (b)

    Elaborate why wing designs based on elliptical circulation
    distribution have fallen out of favor in modern days.

    Disadvantages of an elliptical wing:

    • Elliptical wings are difficult to manufacture due to curved edges
    • Shape of wing ribs vary in a non-uniform way along the wingspan
    • Elliptical wing with a uniform airfoil section can cause the entire wing to
      stall simultaneously, resulting in sudden loss of control with little warning

    Change in speed regime of modern aircraft:

    • Elliptical wings are most efficient at subsonic speeds (low induced drag)
    • Modern aircraft typically operate in transonic/supersonic speed regime
    • At high speeds, shockwave management becomes a critical factor
    • Swept wings, delta wings, serve to minimize impact of shocks by reducing
      the strength of shocks formed, as well as delaying the formation of shocks
    • Spanwise flow of swept wings allow for higher critical Mach numbers Mcr​

    #Part (c)

    Elaborate why military aircraft have much shorter wing spans then civilian aircraft.

    Military aircraft:

    • Wings of military aircraft are optimized for both transonic and supersonic speeds
    • To achieve higher speeds, wings need to be highly swept such that the formation
      of shockwaves can be delayed as much as possible; higher critical Mach numbers
    • At the same time, the wing must generate sufficient lift even at subsonic speeds
    • Highly swept wings inevitably results in a shorter wing span

    Civilian aircraft:

    • Civilian aircraft typically operate in the transonic regime
    • Wings are optimized for aerodynamic efficiency (high lift-to-drag ratio)
    • Induced drag decreases with increase in aspect ratio of the wing, CDi​​=πeARCL​2​
    • A wider wing span also allows for more fuel storage, and thus, more range

    #Part (d)

    Modern civilian aircraft have numerous high-lift and stall-delaying devices
    incorporated into their main wings. While they provide beneficial improvements to
    the aerodynamic characteristics of the aircraft, elaborate upon their disadvantages.

    Disadvantages of devices:

    • Deployment of flaps decrease the stall angle of the wing
    • Flaps increase drag of the aircraft (not fully deployed during takeoff)
    • Slotted Fowler flaps are mechanically complex, which adds additional weight
    • Complexity makes maintenance and repair more difficult, which drives up cost

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    #Part (i)

    Recommend an experimental technique to measure the global pressure
    distribution along the entire test model surface and explain its procedures.

    Pressure sensitive paint:

    • Paint is calibrated by exposing a coated surface to known pressure conditions to establish a relationship between the intensity of the emitted light and the local pressure (pressure-luminance relation; calibration curve)
    • To measure pressure, an excitation light source illuminates the coated surface with light of a specific wavelength that excites the paint and causes it to emit fluorescent light
    • Intensity of emitted light is proportional to the pressure at that location
    • A camera captures the light to obtain pressure distribution on the surface

    #Part (ii)

    Recommend an experimental technique to visualize the
    flow field around the test model and explain its procedures.

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant, tracer particles
    • Laser light source creates a thin light sheet that illuminates the area
    • High-speed camera records motion of suspended particles within the area
    • Cross-correlation is carried out on the images to determine particles’ velocity
    • Calculated velocity vectors are used to obtain the velocity field of the flow

    #Part (iii)

    Particle-image velocimetry was proposed to measure the global velocity field
    around the test model. Explain whether this is an appropriate approach.

    Particle image velocimetry is inappropriate:

    • Aircraft model is tested in a supersonic wind tunnel at Mach 2
    • Requires an extremely fast high-speed camera and laser pulse generator
    • Main disadvantage of particle image velocity is its low frequency response
    • When performing cross-correlation, time interval between each image may be too large, such that velocity obtained is inaccurate, since velocity computed in this manner is an average, rather than instantaneous velocity

    Laser doppler velocimetry is more appropriate:

    • Main advantage of laser doppler velocimetry it its high frequency response
    • Makes use of the frequency shift of lasers to determine particles’ velocity
    • Velocity data can be obtained by performing a Fast Fourier Transform

    #Part (c)

    Explain why such projectiles are typically designed with
    blunt tips rather than sharp tips as shown in the figure.

    • Blunt tip results in the formation of a detached bow shockwave
    • Detached shock minimizes the transmission of vibrations to the projectile
    • Less vibrations reduce the chances of the projectile tumbling (more stable)

    #Part (d)

    Explain why viscous flow behavior should actually be taken into
    account instead of relying entirely on shock-expansion theory.

    Shear stress is defined as τ=μdydu​, where μ is the dynamic viscosity of the fluid.
    At higher speeds, the numerator du becomes very large, and amplifies the effect
    of viscosity on the shear stress experienced by a surface. Thus, viscosity becomes significant at high speeds.
